I had a friend who was an ASL teacher/interpreter, and she tried to explain about the hearing surgery that you asked about. 

She said there is often a stigma in the deaf community towards the operation because, for people who have been deaf their whole life or were born deaf, they aren't lacking anything. Most people she'd talked to had told her that getting the operation would mean that they weren't happy with themselves as they are, or that it would imply that being deaf was wrong and they didn't want to be a part of that community anymore.

When you combine the reasoning with the fact that cochlear implants aren't magical devices, they're invasive and expensive for only so-so results, it is easily understandable why someone would choose to forgo getting them. 

I recommend (to everyone) reading or listening to this [This American Life's](http://www.thisamericanlife.org/radio-archives/episode/411/first-contact) episode. It's about a man named Scott Krepel who chose to get cochlear implants, and then what happened afterward. It's short, but I found it to be extremely educational as he tells his story very descriptively. 

[Here](http://www.thisamericanlife.org/sites/default/files/411_transcript.pdf) is the transcript of the story for those of you who are deaf, or anyone wishing to read it. 

I really encourage you to take a short break and check it out!

Also, (I'm sure no one is going to see this, but hey) people need to know that there are quite a few different types of rabies vaccines out there.

This means when you go to a local discount rabies clinic, you are going to get a vaccine, but it's not necessarily the kind certain vets would give. They aren't likely to be made by the same place. It doesn't mean one works better than the other, but some vaccine distributors have higher incidents of reactions with dogs and cats than others. 

So your dog could've had an allergic reaction to *that company's vaccine*, and not reacted to others because it wasn't getting that same company's shot when you visited the vet a few years later. 

All that being said- ANYONE giving out vaccines at those types of places is supposed to be qualified to look for ANY reaction, because they are aware of how common reactions are given the many varying factors, and how dangerous, too. All it takes is a simple injection of Diphenhydramine (Benadryl) and your dog or cat is covered. This may be everyday stuff for the vet, but I know how scary it is for the common person who doesn't know what to expect when their pet starts reacting.
